message.content: The hedgehog with glasses was the only real creature in a world that had mistaken itself for a painting. His name was Odo, though no one had ever spoken it aloud. He had forty-three quills, a pink nose, and two round brass spectacles that he had found inside a swirl of turquoise. Around him, the world was not made of trees or roads, but of broad strokes, broken grids, floating ovals, and colors that shifted like memory. A field of amber stretched to one side, interrupted by a jagged black line. On the other side, a pale blue rectangle hung in midair, edged with silver. Nothing moved, yet everything seemed to argue for a style. Odo’s glasses did not improve his vision; they made him responsible for meaning. When he put them on, the abstract shapes gained edges. The turquoise swirl became a doorway. The jagged black line became a fence. The pale blue rectangle became a window that looked onto nothing. Without the glasses, the world was only pattern. With them, it became a place he could cross. He told himself this was not imagination, because imagination belonged to creatures, and creatures were real. Still, he knew the truth: the glasses were not correcting the world. They were asking it to behave. In a place made of symbols, loneliness had a texture, and Odo felt it as a fine gray dust on his quills. He walked for what might have been an hour or a century, because time here was a thin brown smear across the upper left corner. He called to a red triangle. “Is anyone real?” he asked. The triangle did not answer, but its color deepened, as if offended. He passed a cluster of small white dots and imagined they were stars, or rain, or the punctuation of a sentence no one had finished. The silence was not empty. It was composed. It had balance, contrast, and rhythm. It simply lacked a creature. To be the only real thing in an abstract world was to become the subject the picture had been avoiding. As Odo moved, the world began to adjust. His footprints did not make holes; they made tiny, precise circles, each one darker at the center, like eyes. The black line bent slightly to let him pass. The turquoise swirl narrowed into a path. Even the gray dust on his quills arranged itself into a faint outline of a hedgehog. He understood then that he had not been merely looking at art. The art had been waiting for something to look back. He pushed one brass rim up with his nose, stepped forward, and became the first real edge in a landscape made of beautiful, unfinished questions.
